signals.excerpt:
# ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building

Can agents build whole products one feature at a time?

Published:

Oct 28, 2026

Preeya Kirani

Daniel Furman

Peter Zhong

Michele Catasta

Today we’re releasing ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software development. It joins the Specialized Intelligence Index (SII) from Fireworks [1], our partner for open-weight model inference and training. The SII brings together practitioner-built benchmarks to compare open, closed, and specialized models on real work tasks across industries.

Most coding benchmarks, like DeepSWE [2], hand an agent a well-defined task inside an existing codebase. In ViBench 2.0, the agent starts with an empty project instead. It then builds a whole product one feature at a time, modeled on products like Uber, GitHub, or Google Docs.

ViBench 2.0 has seventeen products, 241 feature requests, and 544 test plans. The best models, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5, pass all test plans in only 49⁠-⁠65% of their builds.

...

## How the models compare

The official ViBench 2.0 results come from Fireworks’ runs: four builds of the seventeen products per model, on the same harness and settings.

Pass@1 Plan pass rate Cost Build time

### ViBench 2.0: pass@1 against cost per build

Mean of 4 builds of each of 17 products. Whiskers are 95% intervals.

Pass@1 is the share of builds in which every test plan passes, averaged over four builds of each product.

GPT-6.1 Sol leads with a pass@1 of 65%, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 60% and Opus 5.5 at 49%. All three pass more than 90% of their test plans, so most of their failed builds miss by only a few plans. Sol costs about $12 per build, and Astra about $90. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash passes 77% of its test plans for about $2.50 per build, though no open-weight model passes a full build. Opus 5.5 finishes a build in about 70 minutes on average, roughly 2.5 times faster than Sol. Opus produces only about 6% fewer tokens, so the gap mostly comes from API provider speed.

signals.title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
# Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK

by Prabhakar Chandrasekaran and Siddhant Sahu on 26 OCT 2026 in Advanced (300), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Technical How-to Permalink Share

This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated.

It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question, and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen.

Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works.

...

From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation. The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository, so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.

signals.title: 3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary.

Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs:

- Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels to improve execution of the routed-expert computation.
- Online FP8 quantization of the output layer, or LM head, to reduce its weight-read volume.
- Multi-token prediction (MTP) speculative decoding with NEXTN to draft and verify multiple tokens together.

This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook.

...

## Optimization 2: Online FP8 LM head quantization

In the checkpoint, the LM head is stored in BF16 and listed in modules_to_not_convert, so it is not quantized during loading. Its vocabulary GEMM is 157,184 × 2,560, and the entire weight block must be read for each generated token. Under a bandwidth bottleneck, it is therefore a high-value target for compression.

The optimization applies a dynamic FP8 quantization configuration only when constructing the LM head. The rest of the model continues to load with the checkpoint’s FP8/MXFP4 configuration. Moving the LM-head weights from BF16 to FP8 halves the read volume for this layer. The configuration is enabled with SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1.

This setting is mutually exclusive with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option, which outputs logits in FP32 and uses a slower vocabulary-GEMM path.

| Configuration | TPOT | Decode throughput | Relative to baseline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | 27.71 ms | 36.09 tok/s | — |
| + Humming MoE backend | 25.35 ms | 39.45 tok/s | +9.3% |
| + Online FP8 LM head | 22.76 ms | 43.94 tok/s | +21.7% |

Table 2. Cumulative effects of Humming and online FP8 LM-head quantization on NVIDIA DGX Spark, using a synthetic workload with 32K input tokens, 2K output tokens, and batch size 1. Adding FP8 increases decode throughput by 11.4% over Humming alone

...

## Conclusion

Across the full GSM8K evaluation, the three optimizations increased decode throughput by 42.5%, reduced mean end-to-end latency by 24.5%, and produced no statistically detectable accuracy change. Their mechanisms do not overlap: Humming and the FP8 LM head reduce the cost of each step, while MTP reduces the number of steps, so the techniques can be combined.

Stacking, however, is not automatic. Each optimization worked independently, but enabling all three required the draft model to share the full LM-head module. Otherwise, the system silently degrades to a configuration slower than the unoptimized baseline. During deployment, validate that every optimization is active at startup; this is more reliable than

More ways to bring frontier intelligence into the work you do every day.

Update on September 29, 2026: Learn about OpenAI's latest model: GPT‑6 .1 Sol⁠⁠.

Earlier this month, we introduced GPT‑6 Astra, the most intelligent and aligned model in the world. While the most demanding and important projects still call for Astra’s full depth, work happens at different scales, rhythms, and budgets.

That’s why we’re expanding the GPT‑6 universe with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna. GPT‑6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence—these models help distribute the benefits of that intelligence by advancing the frontier on cost efficiency. We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing. Together, these improvements make advanced AI practical for more everyday tasks and applications at scale.

...

### Coding

This year, coding agents have begun tackling tasks with more complexity, scope, and duration than ever before. At OpenAI, our internal usage has grown exponentially. Valued at API prices, daily token usage has exceeded $600 for the median researcher and $7,000 for researchers at the 90th percentile (Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI⁠). As coding agents take on longer and more demanding tasks, the cost of sustained use matters more. GPT‑6 Sol and Luna combine strong coding performance with lower API prices, giving developers more room to iterate and teams the confidence to be more ambitious about what they ask Codex to take on.

On FrontierCode, which evaluates whether coding agents produce changes ready to merge into real codebases, GPT‑6 Sol improves substantially over GPT‑5.6 Sol, and is able to match Claude Fable 5.1 xhigh at much lower cost.

In FrontierCode 1.1 Main⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents write code that’s graded not only on correctness but also “mergeability”: e.g., test quality, scope discipline, code style, and adherence to codebase standards.

On DeepSWE v1.1, which tests performance on complex software-engineering tasks in real codebases, GPT‑6 Sol at max effort scores 68.8%, within 1.1 percentage points of Claude Fable 5’s highest score in the evaluation—69.9% at xhigh effort—at approximately 80% lower cost per task.

GPT‑6 Luna at max effort scores 66.6%, comparable to Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 at medium effort. In these comparisons, Luna costs 93% less per task than Opus 5 and 96% less than Fable 5.

In DeepSWE 1.1⁠(opens in a new window), AI agents solve original, long-horizon software engineering tasks.

...

## Availability

GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access GPT‑6 Luna in the desktop app. These models are not yet available in Chat. In the OpenAI API, they are available as `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-6-luna`.

To keep service stable for everyone, we plan to roll out these models in ChatGPT gradually throughout the day. If you don’t see the new models in ChatGPT Work or Codex, please try again later.

Sulci 1.0: a context-aware semantic cache for agents, and the number most caches don’t publish - DEV Community

 Posted on Oct 27 • Edited on Oct 28 

# Sulci 1.0: a context-aware semantic cache for agents, and the number most caches don’t publish 

### Stable library, hosted tier generally available, every benchmark figure reproducible from the public repo 

Today Sulci is 1.0, and the hosted tier is generally available.

Sulci is an open-source, context-aware semantic cache for LLM apps and AI agents. When a new query means the same thing as a past one, you get the cached answer instead of another model call, even when the words are different. It's Apache 2.0, it runs on infrastructure you already have, and it's three lines around an existing call.

...

## It remembers the conversation 

Sulci is context-aware. Pass a `session_id` and each lookup blends the current query with the conversation's recent turns: 70% the query, 30% a decaying history. "How do I fix it?" after a Docker crash and "How do I fix it?" after a billing error search with two different vectors.

We're careful about what that does and doesn't promise. Blending changes where a follow-up searches; it doesn't make a stored follow-up belong to one conversation. On our corpus, on MiniLM, it didn't measurably improve resolution accuracy (more below). So the hosted tier adds two guards:

- Blended lookups have to clear a stricter bar (0.80, against 0.65 for plain lookups).
- A follow-up that only makes sense inside its conversation is

...

## Adopt it without rewriting anything 

Whatever your agent stack looks like, there's a door that costs a line or less:

| You have | You add |
| --- | --- |
| LangChain or LangGraph | `set_llm_cache(SulciCache(backend="sqlite"))`: one line, every LLM call and graph node cached |
| LlamaIndex | wrap your LLM in `SulciCacheLLM` and pass `session_id=` |
| LiteLLM | `from sulci.integrations.litellm import install` and call it; LiteLLM's 100+ providers are now cached |
| Any OpenAI or Anthropic client, in any language | `pip install "sulci[proxy]"`, run `sulci-proxy` and set `OPENAI_BASE_URL` / `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`. No code change. Hits come back with `x-sulci-cache: hit` |
| An agent that can't import Python | `pip install "sulci[mcp]"` for `sulci-mcp`, an MCP server (stdio, SSE or streamable HTTP, with a read-only mode) |
| TypeScript, Go, Java… | `npm install @sulci/sulci`, or the HTTPS API |

The same `session_id` carries through the library, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, the proxy (as an `x-sulci-session-id` header), the MCP server, the TypeScript client and the HTTP API. Storage is SQLite to start, then Chroma, Qdrant,

# PyTorch 2.15 Release Blog

Source: https://pytorch.org/blog/pytorch-2-15-release-blog/

Last updated: 2026-10-28

---

We are excited to announce the release of PyTorch® 2.15 (release notes)!

The PyTorch 2.15 release features the following changes:

- Rewritten NCCL backend becomes the default, with a flight recorder that dumps on hangs and `TORCH_DIST_USE_NCCL2=0` or `nccl-legacy` as rollback paths
- One-sided transports for torch.distributed, with a NIXL backend and CUDA-graph-capturable transfers
- **FSDP2 and pipelining gain finer memory and communication control,**with fp32 for precision-sensitive parameters, CUDA-graph-captured gradient accumulation, and gradient reduction overlapped with compute 
-   Faster 4-bit (NVFP4) LLM decoding on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs through fewer, better-overlapped kernel launches in NVGEMM
- Apple Silicon gains FP8 and faster decode, with `float8_e4m3fn` and `_scaled_mm`, a new grouped_mm with a decode fast path (1.32–1.34x tokens/s on MoE decode), and public `torch.mps.Stream` APIs
- Broader platform support with FlyDSL kernels on AMD gfx950, Tensor Data Mover support for gfx1250 (MI450), ROCm 10.0 wheels, simpler SYCL kernel authoring and multi-GPU profiling on Intel GPUs, CUDA 13.2 as the default wheel with CUDA 13.4 alongside it, and torch.compile on Python 3.15

### CUDA

#### NVGEMM for NVFP4 Decode

NVGEMM, the CuTeDSL GEMM backend added in 2.14, now folds the scalar dequantization factor of ModelOpt NVFP4 linear layers into the GEMM, removing a separate pointwise launch per layer during decode. A bounded, shape-aware candidate policy covers Blackwell NVFP4 decode shapes that nvMatmulHeuristics misses, and NVGEMM kernels can use programmatic dependent launch so a Triton consumer overlaps with the tail of the producer GEMM. NVGEMM also moves onto CUTLASS Operators.

signals.title: AI agents on a short leash: PipesHub searches company knowledge | heise online
signals.excerpt:
) 

 Oct 28, 2026 at 2:40 pm CET 

 By 

- Moritz Förster

 Contents 

The developers behind the open-source platform PipesHub have released version 1.0.0. The system connects scattered corporate knowledge from services such as Slack, Jira, GitHub and Microsoft 365 for internal searches and AI agents. The first major release introduces, among other things, code graphs for repository analysis, tighter guardrails for AI tools and a revamped search pipeline. The developers have also strengthened permission checks and removed some legacy authentication components.

...

### Permission-Aware Search

PipesHub is an open-source, self-hosted alternative to commercial enterprise search services such as Glean. The system, developed on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, is aimed at companies and development teams that want to make internal data sources searchable or provide them as context for large language models and AI agents without sending data to third-party cloud environments. The software connects to existing systems through more than 50 connectors and inherits their access permissions (permission-aware search). Anyone who isn’t allowed to see a document in Google Drive or a ticket in Jira also won’t receive information from it through PipesHub or connected AI assistants. The system includes citations in its answers, down to individual text passages.

Technically, the platform combines a vector database (Qdrant) for similarity searches with a graph database — Neo4j or ArangoDB by default — as well as MongoDB. With this knowledge graph approach, PipesHub captures not only similar text passages but also structural relationships between documents, users and systems. For language models, the project says on its website it follows a “Bring Your Own Model” approach: Administrators can connect APIs from providers such as OpenAI or Anthropic, or run local models through Ollama. External tools such as Claude Code or Cursor can access the knowledge context through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or SDKs for Python, TypeScript and Go.

...

### Tighter controls for AI agents and new connectors

Because AI agents in PipesHub can do more than read — they can also use tools to trigger actions in connected systems — version 1.0.0 tightens access controls. Agents can now be strictly limited to their assigned toolsets. Tools that only create or modify data can run directly, while operations that delete data require explicit user approval. If a language model generates its own SQL queries, PipesHub now runs them in read-only mode by default unless approval has been granted. Companies can also use OpenAPI specifications to integrate their own REST APIs as custom actions. The MCP server, enabled by default, now also supports approvals for individual tools.

signals.title: Red Hat ships FP8 and DSpark checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | Batch & Release
signals.excerpt:
Red Hat Inference News Oct 28, 2026

# Red Hat ships FP8 and DSpark checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

Red Hat AI releases optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for the 120B multimodal Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, doubling Hopper throughput and cutting memory in half.

Original editorial illustration. Not a product screenshot or measured result.

Red Hat AI has released optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal mixture-of-experts model designed for long-running agents. The FP8 checkpoints double inference throughput on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising accuracy, according to Red Hat. FP8 quantization also cuts model weight memory and storage requirements by half compared with BF16, leveraging Hopper's native FP8 Tensor Core support, which provides roughly twice the matrix-multiply throughput of BF16.

...

## Quantization details

The quantized checkpoints were generated using the LLM Compressor library with a model-free post-training quantization workflow. Quantization is applied to attention, expert, and Mamba projection layers, while shared experts, routers, normalization, and the lm_head remain in BF16. For multi-token prediction layers, attention, expert, and shared expert are quantized, but normalization and the eh_proj layer stay BF16. A creation script in the model card makes the FP8 quantization process fully reproducible.

Red Hat evaluated the FP8 checkpoint on four NVIDIA H200 GPUs using vLLM version 0.31.0, with Inspect AI and Harbor frameworks and non-greedy sampling. The FP8 checkpoint consistently preserves model accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks, the company reports.

...

## DSpark speculative decoding

DSpark speculative decoding drafts 8 to 16 tokens in a single forward pass. It adds a lightweight Markov head to introduce dependencies between speculated tokens, yielding higher-quality candidate sequences and increased inference throughput. Benchmarks on four NVIDIA H100 GPUs used HumanEval, math_reasoning, and RAG datasets.

Replacing the BF16 checkpoint with FP8 primarily boosts aggregate throughput under load. Swapping the MTP speculator for DSpark at BF16 mainly improves single-user streaming speed. Combining FP8 quantization and DSpark outperforms each alone at every concurrency level, according to Red Hat.

...

## Availability

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL models are available via Red Hat Inference Hub on Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA. The optimized checkpoints target inference engineers serving large multimodal models on Hopper hardware, offering a path to higher throughput and lower memory footprint without retraining.

signals.excerpt:
# Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

OCT. 28, 2026

 Google AI Edge Team 

 Android ML Team 

LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

...

### CompiledModel API

 LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

- Simpler: one workflow for CPU and GPU acceleration instead of a different delegate and setup path for each accelerator. LiteRT uses OpenCL where available and OpenGL otherwise. If you request both GPU and CPU, it falls back to CPU on devices without a usable GPU.
- Faster: powered by ML Drift, LiteRT's latest, open-source GPU engine already used by Google apps on millions of devices daily. GPU inference runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy TensorFlow Lite GPU delegate.
- Portable: cross-platform support, so the same `.tflite` model runs on Android, iOS, desktop, and web.
- Flexible: the legacy Interpreter API is still supported on CPU, so you can migrate in phases.

signals.excerpt:
# Nace AI Releases Drex for Search for AI Agents: 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus With 12.6 Search Calls

By

Asif Razzaq

October 26, 2026

Nace AI has released Drex for Search, which brings its Drex decision models to document search. Drex for Search is a retrieval layer that helps people and agents find evidence. Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode call it through CLI, SDKs, MCP or REST. In Nace’s evaluation, it scores 92.05% on BrowseComp-Plus with GPT-5, using 12.6 search calls per question.

...

## How does Drex for Search work inside an agent?

Nace describes 3 steps:

1. Classify: Before any search runs, Drex decides if the question needs a quick lookup or an agent. The agent route reads documents and queries tables.
2. Squeeze: Drex walks the workspace level by level: folder, file, section, page. Inside a sheet, it narrows to table and column. Each level keeps only what can hold the answer.
3. Answer: Only the kept pages and tables reach the LLM. The answer cites the file and page.

Depth is fixed, so Nace says a million files take as many steps as a thousand.

...

## How can developers get access?

Drex for Search runs in the Nace API Console, with 4 ways in on one key:

- CLI: nace-cli on PyPI.
- SDKs: nace-sdk for Python and nace-sdk for TypeScript.
- MCP: nace-mcp, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode.
- REST: an OpenAPI spec.

Google and Meta have opened a new route for AI developers who want their PyTorch models to run on Google’s Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs. Released last week, TorchTPU brings those chips into familiar PyTorch workflows, reducing the need to rebuild models in another framework. Announcement

The simplest examples change the target device in ordinary PyTorch code. Serving a model also requires a working combination of hardware, kernels and runtime settings. The project’s tests distinguish a successful model port from a configuration that has undergone repeated serving checks. Paper Support

PyTorch is the software developers use to define and train models. TorchTPU supplies a backend, the implementation that makes its operations execute on TPU hardware. The repository includes optimized implementations of PyTorch operations, a cache of compiled computations, distributed training and model examples. Its public release is version 0.2.0 and requires Python 3.11 or later. The project uses the Apache 2.0 license. The install command deliberately selects the CPU build of PyTorch; the separate TPU package supplies accelerator execution. Code

## What the serving stack has tested

For serving models to users, the project provides vllm-torchtpu, a plugin for the widely used vLLM engine. It preserves PyTorch model definitions while adding TPU-specific kernels, optimized operations for attention and lower-precision arithmetic. Its installation requirements are more specific than the core package: Python 3.12 on a Cloud TPU virtual machine. Serving

Hardware support differs too. The serving repository recommends Ironwood, or TPU v7x, which is checked on every proposed code change and in nightly tests. # PyTorch opens the AI ecosystem to a new class of accelerators

IBM has made Spyre a first-class PyTorch backend, giving developers the same workflows across devices.

In October 2025, IBM and the PyTorch Foundation outlined a plan for deeper Spyre enablement in 2026: treating the accelerator as a first-class PyTorch backend and supporting multi-accelerator scheduling. The latest software ecosystem updates deliver on that promise. Together, torch-spyre, Spyre's vLLM plugin, compiler improvements, and continuous integration work are making it easier to bring familiar models and workflows to a different class of AI hardware.

...

Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs.

# South Korea's Kakao Open-Sources Two Kanana-2 Embedding Models on Hugging Face 

 Asia Today Published Oct 29, 2026 · 12:41 AM 

 South Korean technology company Kakao has released two open-source AI embedding models, Kanana-2-3b-embedding and Kanana-2-1.3b-embedding, to enhance semantic search and personalized AI agents. Developed by the firm's Unified Foundation Model team, the models are based on Kakao's proprietary small language model architecture and are available on Hugging Face under the Kanana Open License for research and commercial use. According to internal evaluations, the models achieved top retrieval performance in Korean and competitive English performance while significantly reducing inference latency and memory requirements.

...

South Korean technology company Kakao announced on October 29, 2026, the open-source release of two artificial intelligence embedding models designed to enhance semantic search and power personalized AI agents, according to reporting by Asia Today. The two models, named Kanana-2-3b-embedding and Kanana-2-1.3b-embedding, feature 3 billion and 1.3 billion parameters respectively, and have been made available globally through the machine learning platform Hugging Face.

Developed by Kakao's Unified Foundation Model team, the models convert text into numerical representations to evaluate semantic similarity between queries and stored information. Unlike conventional generative language models that synthesize answers directly, embedding models enable systems to identify and retrieve relevant documents or past interactions even when exact matching keywords are absent. To create the suite, Kakao adapted its proprietary small language model, Kanana-2-SLM, to information retrieval tasks for the 3-billion-parameter version, and then applied knowledge distillation to compress that capability into the smaller 1.3-billion-parameter model. Kakao also integrated Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), an architectural technique allowing engineers to adjust embedding vector sizes to balance search precision against storage and processing constraints.

...

Why it matters

The release provides developers and enterprises with specialized, resource-efficient embedding models that lower the hardware barrier for deploying retrieval-augmented generation in non-English contexts. For small and medium-sized enterprises and organizations with limited compute resources, the models' support for vector size scaling via Matryoshka Representation Learning can reduce storage and inference costs for local semantic search. Additionally, open access to high-performing Korean and English embeddings helps diminish reliance on proprietary closed-source API providers for enterprise knowledge retrieval.

signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA TensorRT dramatically accelerates Stable Diffusion 3.5 on RTX GPUs

14 June 2025, 23:26· 1 min read

The rise of generative artificial intelligence models has transformed digital creativity but also increased hardware demands, especially for VRAM. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, a leading image generation model, originally required over 18GB of VRAM, restricting its usability to only a handful of high-end systems. NVIDIA has addressed this limitation by collaborating with Stability AI to quantize the model to FP8—a process that trims VRAM usage by 40%, making it possible for more systems to run the model effectively.

This optimization, combined with the power of NVIDIA TensorRT, generates significant performance leaps. TensorRT, NVIDIA’s AI inference platform, has been reengineered for RTX AI PCs and now offers just-in-time, on-device engine building. Alongside reduced VRAM use, quantized Stable Diffusion 3.5 models see performance more than double, with FP8 TensorRT delivering a 2.3x speedup and 40% lower memory use compared to baseline PyTorch implementations in BF16. Medium versions are also optimized, with a 1.7x increase in speed. These advances allow image creation and editing tasks to proceed quickly and in real time, even on RTX GPUs with less VRAM.

TensorRT for RTX is now available as a standalone software development kit, letting developers take advantage of rapid JIT engine creation without the need for training on device-specific packages. The SDK is eight times smaller than before and integrates with Windows ML for streamlined deployment. The optimized Stable Diffusion 3.5 models are live on Hugging Face and will soon be accessible as NVIDIA NIM microservices, further simplifying deployment for developers and creatives. Such coordinated advances mark a vital step in democratizing high-performance generative artificial intelligence, making advanced image synthesis accessible on a much wider range of systems.

Agentic coding has taken off, and token use has skyrocketed with it. Much of that spend goes to finding things in your code rather than writing it. # Hy-Nomas Ships 8B Interactive World Model on a Single RTX 4090 

 By Alexis Dufresne · Published October 28, 2026 at 03:30 UTC · Updated October 29, 2026 at 03:47 UTC 

## TL;DR

- A single RTX 4090 running INT8 quantization and CPU offloading covers the model, expanding access well beyond the 8-GPU reference configuration.
- A persistent KV cache carries scene context across turns, enabling continuous multi-segment world generation without re-rendering prior frames.
- Tencent published no technical report at launch; all performance figures come from proprietary benchmarks, blocking independent replication.

Hy-Nomas, an 8B diffusion video world model, generates a 100-second clip at 1280×704 and 24 FPS on a single RTX 4090, with peak GPU memory of 20.53 GiB.

The release, posted on Hugging Face, pairs that inference recipe with pairwise human-evaluation numbers against three baselines. On the multi-turn free-form text benchmark, Hy-Nomas beats LingBot-World v2 75.0% of the time on prompt following and 68.3% on physical plausibility. ...

Weights, training code, and a LoRA adaptation workflow ship together, and the paper demonstrates cinematic and robotics LoRAs trained on roughly 100 and 128 clips respectively. # Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence

OCT 27, 2026

Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3, our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face, our Playground, and the Liquid AI API. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

## Highlights

- More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform our previous LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
- Every modality, one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base. 
- Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision. 
- New flagship in-house vision and audio encoders.
- 256K context window for the text model.
- Made to be specialized: every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

LFM3 instances are ideal candidates for specialized intelligence. Fine-tune them on your own data, and deploy them where your application runs. Enjoy the article.
